title: Languages of the court
hook: he wrote in Braj, Persian and Punjabi

segments.voice: Yesterday, names of weapons: a garland of blades used to name the power that protects. Your line was tools for good.

Over the last two weeks, the readings have quietly changed language underfoot. The letter to the emperor: Persian. The war ballad whose first lines open the Ardas: Punjabi. The swayyas, the praise of the Khalsa, the garland of weapon names: mostly Braj, a literary language of poets in northern India. Three languages, one writer. That's not an accident of translation. Readers see a choice in it, a tongue for each job, and today is about why that matters.
screen: `THE LETTER: PERSIAN.` → `THE BALLAD: PUNJABI.` → `THE POEMS: MOSTLY BRAJ.`

segments.voice: Day eighty-three named these three languages; today, why. Each language is a door into a different room. Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government and letters between powers. So the letter to the emperor went in Persian verse, the language its reader worked in every day. Punjabi was the language of the people at home, of the fields and villages. A var, a ballad of courage, belongs there, so Chandi di Var is in Punjabi, the tongue its listeners breathed in. Braj was the language of poetry across a wide stretch of northern India, the one poets used for devotion and for story. Much of the Guru's longer poetry is in Braj, written in the Gurmukhi script. Jaap Sahib, one of the Sikh morning prayers, is full of names for God, and some readers notice that it draws them from more than one world. Alongside names rooted in Sanskrit, it calls God Razak, the provider, and Rahim, the merciful, words that come from Arabic and Persian. It's the move Akal Ustat and the Zafarnama's opening made, carried into a daily prayer. One God, praised in the vocabularies of neighbors who often didn't share a prayer. For Sikhs that fits a long thread. The Guru Granth Sahib itself gathers voices from many regions and backgrounds. Many tongues, one Name. Language, in this tradition, isn't a fence around the holy. It's a set of doors, and the Guru walked through several of them.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF THE COURT.` · `PUNJABI: THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `BRAJ: THE LANGUAGE OF POETS.` · `ONE GOD, MANY VOCABULARIES.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Pick a word you know in a language that isn't your first, thank you, peace, water, and say it once, quietly, noticing how it sits in your mouth. Then bring to mind the people who say that word every day without thinking, and let them be near for a breath or two; if you pray, follow the word with Waheguru.
Languages of the court. Guru Gobind Singh wrote in Persian for the emperor, Punjabi for the people, and Braj for poetry. Today's word.
Your line: many tongues. Persian, Punjabi and Braj: three languages, one writer. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Guru Gobind Singh's compositions in their original languages, Braj, Persian and Punjabi, usually printed in Gurmukhi script, and teachers explain them in katha in Punjabi, English and other languages.

chat.says: Why did the Guru write in three languages? Couldn't he just pick one?
options: Readers see a choice: Persian for the emperor, Punjabi for the people, Braj for poetry.
He had to: Punjabi had no written script yet, so he borrowed others.
It was chance. Translators later moved his works into different languages.
